title: Students' Perception of Online Disinformation, Misinformation, and Malinformation
screen_reason: Online questionnaire of 109 Croatian university students (Nov 2022 - Jan 2023). Table 13 reports, per study group, how many respondents said they had SHARED disinformation, misinformation and malinformation, with a yes/no/cannot-determine breakdown that reconciles exactly with each group's N. Self-reported sharing of misinformation is an eligible RECALL (recall_subtype=sharing) measure. The paper's frequency-of-encountering items (Table 12) are reported only as mean ranks, so they yield no share and no row.

estimates.country: Croatia (Faculty of Humanities and Social Sciences, Josip Juraj Strossmayer University of Osijek)
estimates.platform: Online Google Forms questionnaire (self-report about online information sources)
estimates.measure_type: % of Information Sciences students who reported having shared misinformation
estimates.value_raw: 25 IS students reported sharing misinformation, of N=51 IS students (25/51 = 49.0%); the paper prints '25 IS students (22.9%)', the 22.9% being of the whole 109-respondent sample
estimates.denominator: 51 Information Sciences (IS) students among the 109 valid respondents at the Faculty of Humanities and Social Sciences in Osijek (25 yes, 11 no, 15 'cannot determine' = 51)
estimates.definition: Respondent answered YES to having shared misinformation, after being given the definitions: 'Misinformation consists of false information, but the person spreading it believes to be true'
estimates.misinfo_def: 'Misinformation consists of false information, but the person spreading it believes to be true. Disinformation, on the other hand, is also false information, but it is deliberately spread with the knowledge that it is untrue. ... malinformation refers to information that is based on truth but is used to cause harm'
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Pure self-report: respondents were given textbook definitions of disinformation, misinformation and malinformation in Q14 and then asked (Q14-18) about their own dissemination habits. No verification, no behavioural data. The authors note self-reported data may be biased and that students may have overestimated their skills.
estimates.moderator_quote: An online Google Forms questionnaire was distributed to undergraduate and graduate students of Information Sciences (IS) and English Language and Literature (ELL) via e-mail and the Faculty's MOODLE platform from November 2022 to January 2023. ... With a 109 valid responses, the response rate was sufficient for analysis. For the purposes of this research, the study groups were divided into IS (N=51), ELL (N=52) and IS-ELL double-major combination (N=6).
estimates.notes: IMPORTANT: the paper NEVER prints a whole-sample sharing rate; every figure in Table 13 is a count with a percentage of the full 109. The value here is an exact part/whole share from two verbatim counts with the same denominator (25 of the 51 IS students), permitted by R8; the group cells reconcile exactly (25+11+15=51). BIG CAVEAT for pooling: a third answer option was 'cannot determine' (15 IS students, 29.4% of the group), so 49.0% is the share answering YES, not the share of a yes/no dichotomy (yes/(yes+no) would be 25/36 = 69.4%, a different denominator, not extracted). Study-group rows are given rather than one overall row because the study-group comparison IS the paper's design and headline (H3, chi-square tests), and the overall total would require summing across groups, which R8 forbids - see missed_or_uncertain. year=2022 as the representative point of a Nov 2022-Jan 2023 field period.  QUOTE NOTE: the v2 text extraction interleaves the article's columns, so no longer contiguous span of the published sentence is recoverable; source_quote is the exact contiguous span carrying the value, and the full published sentence is: "For misinformation, 25 IS students (22.9%), 23 ELL students (21.1%), and 4 IS-ELL students (3.7%) reported sharing it, while 11 IS students (10.1%), 8 ELL students (7.3%), and 1 IS-ELL student (0.9%) denied doing so." (Results 4.4, p. 3555); Table 13 misinformation row for IS reads "IS 25 [22.9] 11 10.1 15 13.8".

missed_or_uncertain: (1) WHOLE-SAMPLE TOTALS, deliberately NOT extracted: adding the three mutually exclusive study groups would give 52/109 = 47.7% for misinformation sharing, 16/109 = 14.7% for disinformation and 13/109 = 11.9% for malinformation. The paper never prints these, and R8 forbids cross-category sums, so no total row is created - but they are recorded here because an adjudicator may judge that summing exhaustive subgroups of one sample is admissible. (2) The third study group, IS-ELL double majors, is n=6 (misinformation 4 yes = 66.7%, disinformation 1 yes = 16.7%): too small to be a usable row and the authors themselves flag the group's size as a limitation, so it is not extracted. (3) MALINFORMATION sharing (IS 7/51 = 13.7%, ELL 5/52 = 9.6%) is EXCLUDED on construct grounds: the paper defines malinformation as 'information that is based on truth but is used to cause harm', i.e. true content, which is outside this review's misinformation definition. (4) Table 12 asks how often respondents encounter disinformation/misinformation/malinformation in eight source types on a 1 (never) to 7 (always) scale, but reports ONLY mean ranks by study group (e.g. independent news portals IS 52.23, ELL 55.17, IS-ELL 77.08) with no share of respondents above any threshold, so per the instructions this yields no row - this is the paper's only 'perceived exposure' measure and it is unusable. (5) '66 respondents (60.6%) claimed to have known [the terms] beforehand' is term familiarity, not exposure. (6) Source-use shares (social media 88.1%, online newspapers 67%) and evaluation-habit shares (58.7% evaluate everyday information, 61.5% academic) are media-use and verification behaviours, not misinformation encounters. (7) Externally cited figures ('86% of adults admitted to using social media to obtain news', 'less than 30% stated believing the news they read was true', 32%/50%/68%/71%/61%/33% US figures from Pew) are all from references [16],[17] and are excluded by R8. (8) INTERNAL INCONSISTENCIES an adjudicator should note: Table 1 gives IS = 46.8% of respondents while section 4.1 says 'IS (51, 64.8%)'; the IS-ELL group is printed as '6, 0.1%' (should be ~5.5%); and section 4.3 says '42% (N=38.5) do not evaluate' academic information, an impossible count. These do not affect the Table 13 cells used here, which reconcile exactly with the group Ns.

rob.design: Cross-sectional online questionnaire (19 items, Google Forms) distributed by e-mail and the faculty MOODLE platform from November 2022 to January 2023 to undergraduate and graduate students of Information Sciences and English Language and Literature at a single Croatian faculty; 109 valid responses (IS 51, ELL 52, IS-ELL 6). Response rate reported inconsistently (64.8% for IS, 47.7% for ELL in section 4.1, versus 46.8%/47.7% shares in Table 1). Self-report throughout, with definitions of disinformation/misinformation/malinformation supplied to respondents before the sharing questions and a 'cannot determine' option offered. Analysis in SPSS v26: frequencies, chi-square and Mann-Whitney; all three hypotheses rejected. The single open-ended question yielded only one valid response (N=1). Authors' stated limitations: single-faculty sample not representative of students broadly, self-report bias, small IS-ELL group, and a deliberately short instrument to avoid dropout. No validation of the instrument, no reliability statistics, no weighting.
